newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Britain urged to take China to U.N. over Hong Kong.
newsitem.headline: Britain urged to take China to U.N. over Hong Kong.

text.p: Outspoken Hong Kong legislator Martin Lee urged Britain on Tuesday to resort to the United Nations in a last ditch effort to prevent China rowing back Hong Kong's civil liberties after the handover later this year.

British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind has said Britain would "maintain maximum pressure until June 30" on China to reverse its plans and would continue to monitor developments in its former colony beyond the handover.
But Lee, chairman of the colony's largest party, the Democratic Party, said he had told Rifkind at a meeting in London that that was not enough.

"I told him as a matter of international law, public international law, there is one more thing at least the British government can do, which is to take the matter to the United Nations," Lee told a news conference on his return from a nine-nation European tour.

Lee accused the British of paying lip-service to the terms of the 1984 Sino-British Joint Declaration governing the handover which binds China to preserving Hong Kong's liberties intact for 50 years after the transition at midnight on June 30.
Britain could ask fellow Security Council members to refer China's post-handover political plans to the International Court of Justice (ICJ), Lee said.

Britain has in the past asked China to voluntarily submit to a ruling by the ICJ on the legality of the "provisional legislature" which Beijing has set up to replace Hong Kong's existing, elected council when more than 150 years of British rule ends.
Lee noted that China was also a member of the U.N. Security Council and could veto the proposal, but said such a move would only draw more world attention to Beijing's plans.

"Now that (the veto) is fine, but at least China would have to do something in the full view of the international community by vetoing the referral of an important question which comes about as the result of China's conduct and behaviour in relation to China's own agreement with Britain."
Lee also lashed out at critics, including Hong Kong's future leader Tung Chee-hwa, who denounced him for "bad-mouthing" Hong Kong abroad.
Despite protests from Hong Kong's vocal pro-democracy camp, and from Britain and several allies including the United States, China has pressed on with its plans for Hong Kong.
Its parliament approved a plan on Sunday to throw out or amend a clutch of Hong Kong laws, including those providing for democratic elections and protect civil liberties.
The plan trims back a bill of rights, a law on forming political parties and another on free association which takes a liberal approach to public protests and demonstrations.
Beijing has justified its onslaught on Hong Kong's fledgling democracy by accusing Britain of violating the Joint Declaration by instituting recent democratic reforms.
Lee warned China that its belief that eroding civil and political liberties would not affect prosperity was mistaken and urged the business community to ensure the message reached Beijing's ears.
